stimulus.t: A study of sixty countries found that those whose central banks are legally independent of the government have, on average, markedly lower inflation than those whose central banks are not.
Therefore, granting a central bank legal independence lowers a country’s inflation.

stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on the testimony of an authority whose expertise lies outside the field in question
overlooks the possibility that countries already committed to low inflation are more likely to grant their central banks independence
takes for granted that inflation is the sole measure of a central bank’s performance
treats a condition that is required for low inflation as though it were sufficient to produce it
fails to consider that some countries with independent central banks nonetheless have high inflation

diagram.gap: The correlation reflects central-bank independence causing low inflation, not the reverse and not a common cause.

brief.facts: Countries with independent central banks average lower inflation. The author concludes that independence causes lower inflation.
brief.issue: What is wrong with moving from correlation to causation here?
brief.rule: A correlation between A and B is consistent with A causing B, B causing A, a third factor C causing both, or coincidence. A causal conclusion must rule out the alternatives.

analysis.correct: (B) names reverse causation: an inflation-averse political culture could lead countries to grant independence, rather than independence producing low inflation.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: No authority is cited; the argument relies on a study.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The argument concerns inflation only and never claims to measure overall performance.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: A plausible-sounding conditional confusion, but the argument draws a causal inference, not a conditional one.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Averages tolerate exceptions. A few high-inflation independent banks do not damage a claim about the general effect.

brief.holding: Correlation → causation is always vulnerable to reverse causation and common cause; look for the answer that names one of them.

stimulus.t: An online survey of subscribers to the journal Arbitration Quarterly found that 82 percent prefer arbitration to litigation for resolving cross-border commercial disputes.
Clearly, most businesses engaged in cross-border commerce prefer arbitration.

stem: The argument is most vulnerable to which one of the following criticisms?
choices: It confuses how widespread a preference is with how strongly it is held.
It fails to establish that arbitration is in fact superior to litigation.
It draws a conclusion about a large population from a sample that is likely to be biased toward a particular response.
It assumes that a preference held by most members of a group is held by every member.
It takes for granted that subscribers to the journal are not engaged in cross-border commerce.

diagram.gap: Arbitration Quarterly subscribers are representative of all cross-border businesses.

brief.facts: 82% of a specialist arbitration journal’s subscribers prefer arbitration. Conclusion: most cross-border businesses prefer arbitration.
brief.issue: Is the sample representative of the population in the conclusion?
brief.rule: A sample supports a generalization only if it is representative. Self-selected or specialist samples are suspect.

analysis.correct: (C) Readers of an arbitration journal are far more likely than typical businesses to favor arbitration. The sample is skewed toward the very response measured.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Intensity of preference is never at issue.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The conclusion concerns what businesses PREFER, not which method is better.

wrong.label: shell-game
wrong.why: The conclusion says ‘most,’ not ‘every.’

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: The argument, if anything, assumes they are representative of such businesses.

brief.holding: Ask WHO was surveyed and whether that group leans toward the answer being measured.

stimulus.t: Commentator: Any program that increases the money supply is inflationary,
and because inflation erodes the value of savings, every inflationary program is in effect a tax.
The central bank’s new lending program increases the money supply,
so it is a tax.
Since the constitution permits only the legislature to impose taxes, the lending program is unconstitutional.

stem: The reasoning in the commentator’s argument is flawed because the argument
choices: takes for granted that every increase in the money supply is inflationary
concludes that a policy is undesirable merely because it has some negative effects
presumes that what is true of a program as a whole is true of each of its parts
shifts from using a key term in an economic sense to using it in a legal sense
infers a causal relationship from a mere correlation

diagram.gap: A ‘tax’ in the economic sense is a ‘tax’ in the constitutional sense.

brief.facts: Money creation → inflation → an economic burden the commentator calls a ‘tax.’ The constitution reserves ‘taxes’ to the legislature, so the program is unconstitutional.
brief.issue: Does ‘tax’ mean the same thing throughout?
brief.rule: Equivocation: a word changes meaning between premise and conclusion, so the premises connect only verbally.

analysis.correct: (D) ‘In effect a tax’ is an economic metaphor; the constitutional clause concerns taxes as a legal category. The argument trades on the shift.

wrong.label: restatement
wrong.why: This is a stated premise. Flaw questions accept the premises; the error lies in the inference.

wrong.label: shell-game
wrong.why: The conclusion is about constitutionality, not desirability.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: No whole-to-part reasoning occurs.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: No correlation is offered.

brief.holding: Hedges like ‘in effect’ or ‘in a sense’ often mark the moment a word quietly changes meaning.

stimulus.t: Only companies whose accounts have been audited for three consecutive years may list on the exchange’s premium tier.
Zentara Corp.’s application for the premium tier was rejected.
Hence Zentara’s accounts have not been audited for three consecutive years.

stem: The flawed reasoning in the argument is that the argument
choices: confuses a company’s audit history with the quality of its accounts
draws a general conclusion about all listed companies from a single case
fails to consider that some companies on the premium tier have not been audited for three consecutive years
overlooks the possibility that a company could satisfy a necessary condition for premium listing and still be refused
assumes that the exchange applies its listing rules consistently

diagram.gap: Being audited for three years guarantees premium listing.

brief.facts: Premium → audited three years. Zentara was not admitted. The author concludes that Zentara was not audited three years.
brief.issue: Does failing the outcome mean failing the requirement?
brief.rule: From A → B, the fact ¬A tells you nothing about B (the negation fallacy). A necessary condition can be met while the outcome still fails.

analysis.correct: (D) Zentara may have met the audit requirement but failed some OTHER condition. Meeting a necessary condition does not guarantee the outcome.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Account quality is never mentioned.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The conclusion is about Zentara alone.

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: That would contradict the premise, and flaw answers must not attack premises.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Consistency of enforcement is not the problem; the logic fails even with perfectly consistent enforcement.

brief.holding: ‘Only X may Y’ makes X necessary. Failing Y never proves failing X.

stimulus.t: Regulator: The food additive tarvanol has been examined in more than a dozen short-term studies,
and none of them established that it harms human health.
We can therefore conclude that tarvanol poses no long-term risk to human health.

stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the regulator’s reasoning?
choices: It treats the failure to establish that a substance is harmful as sufficient grounds for concluding that it is harmless.
It rejects a claim merely because the claim has not been proven with certainty.
It relies on studies conducted by parties with a financial interest in the outcome.
It presumes that a substance harmful in large doses is harmful in small doses.
It generalizes from the effects of tarvanol to the effects of all food additives.

diagram.gap: The absence of evidence of long-term harm is evidence that there is no long-term harm.

brief.facts: Short-term studies found no established harm. Conclusion: no long-term risk.
brief.issue: Does a lack of proof of harm prove safety, especially safety over a time frame the studies never examined?
brief.rule: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, particularly when the evidence-gathering could not have detected the effect in question.

analysis.correct: (A) The regulator moves from ‘not shown harmful’ to ‘shown harmless.’ The studies were short-term, so they could not detect long-term harm at all.

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: The regulator ACCEPTS a claim (safety) without proof; this answer describes the reverse error.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Funding is never mentioned.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Dosage is never discussed.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The conclusion concerns tarvanol only.

brief.holding: Ask whether the investigation could even have found the thing whose absence is being claimed.

stimulus.t: Senator Osei has proposed requiring large banks to hold more capital in reserve.
Evidently, the senator believes that banks should be prevented from lending altogether.
But lending is essential to economic growth,
so the senator’s proposal should be rejected.

stem: The argument is flawed in that it
choices: concludes that a proposal will have a certain effect merely because it was intended to have that effect
treats evidence that lending is essential as proof that all lending is beneficial
relies on a premise that merely restates its conclusion
attacks the senator’s character rather than the substance of her proposal
distorts a proposal into a more extreme position and then argues against that position

diagram.gap: Higher capital reserves amount to prohibiting lending.

brief.facts: The senator proposes higher capital reserves. The author recasts this as a wish to ban lending, then rejects it because lending fuels growth.
brief.issue: Is the author arguing against what the senator actually proposed?
brief.rule: Straw man: misrepresent the opposing position, usually as more extreme, then refute the misrepresentation.

analysis.correct: (E) Raising reserve requirements is not banning lending. The author refutes a position the senator never took.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Intended effects are not discussed.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: No claim about ALL lending being beneficial is made.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The premises do not restate the conclusion.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Her character is never attacked; her position is misdescribed.

brief.holding: ‘Evidently, X believes …’ followed by an extreme paraphrase is a straw-man alarm.

stimulus.t: Every clause in the proposed trade agreement is easy to understand.
So the agreement itself is easy to understand.

stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: The committee as a whole is divided on the issue. So each of its members must be undecided.
Every member of the delegation speaks Hungarian. So the delegation can conduct its negotiations in Hungarian.
Each witness testified credibly. So at least one witness gave credible testimony.
Most of the firm’s partners favor the merger. So the firm will approve the merger.
Every chapter of the treatise is concise. So the treatise is concise.

diagram.gap: A property of each part (easy to understand) belongs to the whole.

brief.facts: Each clause is easy → the agreement is easy. But clauses can interact in complex ways.
brief.issue: Which answer commits the same part-to-whole error?
brief.rule: Composition flaw: infer that a whole has a property because each part has it, when the property may not transfer.

analysis.correct: (E) Concise chapters can still add up to a long treatise. Parts → whole, with a property that does not transfer.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: Whole-to-part (division), the reverse direction, and a different inference.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Reasonable, not flawed. A shared language of all members does transfer to the group’s capacity.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Valid: if each is credible, at least one is.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: A different gap: whether partner preference determines firm approval.

brief.holding: In Parallel Flaw, match the DIRECTION of the error (parts → whole) and confirm the property really fails to transfer.

stimulus.t: It is possible that regulators will block the proposed merger.
If the merger is blocked, Halden’s share price will fall.
So Halden’s share price will fall.

stem: Which one of the following exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to the argument above?
choices: If the river floods, the bridge will close. The bridge has closed. So the river must have flooded.
The vote can pass only if the delegates attend. The delegates might attend. So the vote might pass.
Most years, the harbor freezes in January. It is now January. So the harbor will probably freeze.
The tenants’ association may call a strike. If it calls a strike, the landlord will negotiate. Therefore, the landlord will negotiate.
The court will hear the appeal this term. If it hears the appeal, the ruling might be reversed. So the ruling might be reversed.

brief.facts: A possible event (merger blocked) would cause a result (price fall). The author concludes the result WILL occur.
brief.issue: Which answer also turns a possibility into a certainty?
brief.rule: Possibility vs. certainty: ‘X may happen; if X, then Y; so Y’ is invalid.

analysis.correct: (D) ‘May call a strike’ → ‘will negotiate’ repeats the exact move: a mere possibility treated as an established fact.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: Affirms the necessary condition, a different flaw.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: A different error. Meeting a necessary condition is treated as making the outcome possible, but the conclusion stays modal (‘might’), not certain.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Reasonable probabilistic reasoning.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Valid: certain premise plus a possible consequence yields a possible conclusion.

brief.holding: Track modality: ‘may’ in the premises cannot become ‘will’ in the conclusion.

stimulus.t: Any treaty ratified by the Senate is binding on the federal government.
The Bilateral Water Accord is binding on the federal government.
So the Senate must have ratified it.

stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in the argument above is most closely paralleled in which one of the following?
choices: All certified translators have passed the state examination. Mira is not a certified translator. So Mira has not passed the state examination.
All licensed pilots have passed the medical examination. Reka has not passed the medical examination. So Reka is not a licensed pilot.
Most firms that hire the consultancy see higher profits. Kallos saw higher profits. So Kallos probably hired the consultancy.
Every vintage the estate releases has been aged for five years. This wine has been aged for five years. So the estate must have released it.
Only members in good standing may vote. Bence voted. So Bence is a member in good standing.

brief.facts: Ratified → binding. The Accord is binding. Conclusion: it was ratified.
brief.issue: Which answer commits the same error: affirming the necessary condition and concluding the sufficient one?
brief.rule: From A → B and B, nothing follows about A (the reversal fallacy). Distinguish it from the negation fallacy (from A → B and ¬A, conclude ¬B).

analysis.correct: (D) Released → aged five years. This wine is aged five years. Conclusion: it was released by the estate. Same form: A → B, B, therefore A.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: Flawed, but it is the NEGATION fallacy (¬A → ¬B), not the reversal. Same family, different form.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Valid contrapositive: ¬B → ¬A.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Probabilistic and hedged (‘probably’), a different structure.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Valid: Vote → Good standing, Bence voted, so good standing.

brief.holding: Reversal (B, so A) and negation (¬A, so ¬B) are different flaws. Parallel Flaw requires the same one.
